summary: Explains the design of MOBIKE, an extension of IKEv2 for efficient management of IKE and IPsec security associations when a host has multiple IP addresses or its addresses change. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This explains the reasons behind the design of the protocol that keeps secure tunnels running when a device changes its address.

questions: how does mobike handle ip address changes
how does ipsec work with mobile devices
subtitle: How to keep IPsec tunnels running when a device changes its IP address.

tldr.problem: When a mobile device or multi-homed host changes its IP address, the existing IKEv2 authentication and IPsec encryption associations must be torn down and rebuilt, which is expensive and disruptive, especially if the address changes frequently.
tldr.mechanism: MOBIKE (IKEv2 Mobility and Multihoming) is an extension to IKEv2 that allows the IP addresses associated with an IKE SA and its IPsec SAs to be updated without re-establishing the entire security association. Peers exchange address information and verify connectivity to new addresses before switching.
tldr.outcome: Devices can move to new networks or switch between multiple interfaces while maintaining ongoing encrypted connections, which is essential for mobile devices and multihomed hosts.

today: RFC 4621 is an Informational design document describing the rationale behind MOBIKE. The actual MOBIKE protocol specification is in RFC 4555. Both documents remain current as MOBIKE is used in mobile VPN implementations.

sections.title: The Problem with Changing IP Addresses
sections.content:
IKEv2 (defined in RFC 4306) assumes that the IP address pair used when establishing a security association will stay the same. Each IKE SA is implicitly bound to the source and destination IP addresses used during the initial key exchange, and in tunnel mode, these same IP addresses appear in the outer headers of every encrypted packet.

However, in modern networks, IP addresses change frequently. A mobile device might move from one access point to another, or a laptop might switch between a wired Ethernet connection and WiFi. A multi-homed device (one with multiple network interfaces) might want to switch from one interface to another if the first one fails.

Before MOBIKE, changing an IP address meant tearing down the entire IKE SA and all its associated IPsec SAs, then running a complete new authentication exchange. This is expensive, may require user interaction (such as entering a security token), and creates a window where communication is interrupted. MOBIKE provides a way to update the addresses without this disruption.
sections.eli5: IKEv2 locks your secure connection to one IP address. If you move and get a new address, the old system would disconnect you completely. MOBIKE lets you change addresses and keep the connection alive.

sections.title: Key Concepts in MOBIKE
sections.content:
MOBIKE introduces several important terms. An available address is an address currently assigned to one of your network interfaces and ready to use. A locally operational address is available and also known to work for communication. An operational address pair is a pair of addresses where bidirectional communication between two peers can be demonstrated.

The preferred address of a peer is the IP address that should be used for sending new MOBIKE and IPsec traffic by default. Each peer has only one preferred address at a time. A peer address set is the subset of locally operational addresses that a peer announces to the other peer. Finally, a path is the sequence of routers traversed by packets between two peers, and this path is determined not just by the source and destination IP addresses but also by the transport protocol being used.
sections.eli5: A peer has many addresses it could use, but picks one as preferred. Before switching, it verifies the new address can actually reach the other side. The path is the route packets take.

sections.title: Mobility and Multihoming Scenarios
sections.content:
RFC 4621 describes three main usage scenarios for MOBIKE. In a mobility scenario, a mobile node establishes an IPsec connection to a security gateway (for example, to access a corporate network), then moves to a new access point and obtains a new IP address. MOBIKE allows the mobile node and gateway to continue using their existing security associations rather than re-authenticating.

In a multihoming scenario, each peer has multiple network interfaces with multiple IP addresses, but normally uses one as the preferred address. If that interface fails or becomes unavailable, the peer can switch to another interface by announcing a new preferred address. In a multihomed laptop scenario, a device has many different ways to connect (Ethernet, WiFi, GPRS, Bluetooth), and which interfaces are active depends on cost, availability and user preference. As the laptop connects or disconnects interfaces, the set of IP addresses it is reachable at changes, and MOBIKE coordinates these changes so the IPsec tunnel continues working.
sections.eli5: A phone moving between WiFi networks needs MOBIKE to stay connected. A laptop with both Ethernet and WiFi needs it to switch interfaces. A device with many addresses uses it to pick which one to use.

sections.title: Key Design Decisions
sections.content:
RFC 4621 documents the design considerations that influenced how MOBIKE works. One major decision was address selection: who decides which address pair to use after an address changes? The working group chose that the IKEv2 initiator (the peer that started the key exchange) makes all address selection decisions. This choice ensures both peers use the same address pair (avoiding asymmetric routing), and works best with Network Address Translation devices because the initiator is most likely the device behind a NAT.

Another key design choice was about return routability: before trusting a new address, the other peer should verify the sending peer actually owns that address and can receive replies at it. Without such verification, a malicious peer could redirect all traffic to an unrelated third party. MOBIKE uses IKEv2 informational exchanges with a random nonce as a return routability check.

For IPsec SA updates, the working group decided to move all IPsec SAs together when the IKE SA address changes, rather than allowing individual IPsec SAs to use different address pairs. This simplifies the protocol. If more granular control is needed, multiple separate IKE SAs can be created.
sections.eli5: The device that started the connection decides what address to use. Before switching, it checks the new address actually works. When the tunnel address changes, all the encrypted connections using it switch together.

sections.title: Handling Network Address Translation
sections.content:
Devices behind a Network Address Translation (NAT) device have their private IP addresses rewritten to the NAT's address by the NAT. This complicates MOBIKE because the two peers see different IP addresses: one peer sees the NAT's public address, while the peer behind the NAT sees its own private address.

MOBIKE uses the NAT-T mechanisms from RFC 4306 to detect when a NAT is present and uses UDP encapsulation of ESP packets to traverse the NAT. However, MOBIKE makes one important change to IKEv2: it disables the dynamic address updating for IKE packets, which would interfere with MOBIKE's own address testing mechanisms.

A special design feature of MOBIKE is NAT prevention: if a NAT is detected on a path, that path can be prevented from being used in configurations where no NAT should exist. This protects against on-path attackers who might try to modify IP addresses in headers, since MOBIKE will detect the NAT and reject the path.
sections.eli5: If a NAT (network address translator) is in the way, MOBIKE hides the traffic in UDP packets so it gets through. MOBIKE can also detect if something is secretly changing addresses and refuse to use that path.

sections.title: Protocol Implementation Details
sections.content:
MOBIKE uses standard IKEv2 messaging for address updates, which means both peers must support MOBIKE for it to work. Support is indicated during the IKE_AUTH exchange using a Notify payload. The actual address updates are sent in IKEv2 informational exchanges, with one Notify payload for each address to be communicated.

When address changes are detected, MOBIKE tests connectivity using IKEv2 dead-peer detection on the candidate address pair. Once connectivity is confirmed and return routability is verified, the new address becomes the preferred address for subsequent packets. Because the initiator makes all address decisions, the responder simply accepts the initiator's choice of preferred address.

The RFC documents that MOBIKE currently focuses on tunnel mode (where the outer IP headers change while the inner headers remain constant). Transport mode support is identified as a topic for future work.
sections.eli5: MOBIKE messages are sent using the regular IKEv2 format, with special address-related notifications. It pings the new address to make sure it works, then switches over once everything checks out.
